newsitem.title: UK: UK markets still harbour doubts about Labour.
newsitem.headline: UK markets still harbour doubts about Labour.

text.p: Britain's opposition Labour Party no longer holds so many terrors for London's financial markets but there are lingering areas of concern and no little confusion, analysts said on Tuesday.

They had hoped for Labour's policies to be fleshed out in greater detail at its annual conference in Blackpool but said they were still in the dark over what a Labour government would do in key areas, particularly European monetary union (EMU).
"Labour's priority is to win the election and the best way to do that may be to say as little as possible," said Nigel Richardson, head of bond research at Yamaichi International.
But given that uncertainty, he said UK government bonds -- gilts -- would succumb to political uncertainty in the run-up to elections that must be held by May 1997.

Gilts have already suffered in comparison with other European bond markets in countries pledged to EMU. And unless Labour commits itself to a single currency, offering markets the promise of sustainable lower interest rates and greater stability, a change of government may do little good.
Speaking to a party conference on Tuesday, Labour Party leader Tony Blair said his government would keep its options open on a single currency and would not end Britain's veto.
And earlier in the day, Robin Cook, Labour's foreign affairs spokesman, told BBC radio that a decision on EMU was not needed until late next year.

"The longer-term commitment seems to be there but a decision on EMU is being left rather late for the first round," said Alex Garrard, UK economist at UBS. A first round of European Economic and Monetary Union is scheduled for January 1, 1999.
Indeed, many in Europe now find it difficult to split the ruling Conservative Party and Labour over EMU.

"In many ways, Britain's European trading partners are looking to circumvent the UK position now because not only do they not have any faith in the Tory government's move towards EMU, they don't have that much faith in Labour either," Jeremy Hawkins, senior economic adviser at BankAmerica told Sky TV.
On Monday, shadow finance spokesman Gordon Brown took his turn in front of the Labour Conference.

He scrupulously avoided detailing Labour's stance on EMU but did tell delegates it was time for Britain "to join the civilised industrial world and implement a national minimum wage." He did not specify a level.
That will not go down well with the markets but may not be a disaster.

"The minimum wage is a negative," Garrard said. "But it looks like they will pitch it much lower than the unions want." Earlier this month, the Trades Union Congress demanded a minimum wage be set at 4.26 per hour. Garrard said 3.20 was a more likely level. "And it won't come in before 1998."

Cook used his speech to conference to pledge that a Labour government would sign up to the Social Chapter, which guarantees minimum working conditions for EU workers, by the end of 1997. That commitment will also go down like a lead balloon in the City. "The Social Chapter, in the context of the sort of freedom UK labour markets have at the moment, could be very dangerous," Hawkins said.

On tax, Brown talked of a minimum rate of income tax of 10 to 15 pence as a long-term goal and also said a windfall tax would be levied on Britain's privatised utilities. That vow caused instant jitters on London's stock market on Monday. British electricity and water shares all lost ground.
On the plus side, Brown's commitment to "iron discipline" on public spending will be a source of comfort to Britain's financial markets.
And Blair's statement in Blackpool, that a Labour government would set defined targets for inflation and interest rates to keep them low, although no surprise, will be grist to the markets' mill.
But still, for the City, the jury is out.
"The City is waiting for the real flesh to be put on the bones," said Richard Jeffrey, economist at stockbrokers Charterhouse Tilney. "It's hard to draw any firm conclusions yet."
